emergency.general: Call 911 for all emergencies — police, fire, and ambulance. In areas where 911 is not yet active, call 117 for police. Operators speak Filipino and English. Emergency response times vary significantly between Metro Manila and provincial areas, where reaching a hospital may take considerably longer.

healthcare.summary: Health & medication guide for Philippines. Emergency numbers (911/117), pharmacy tips, restricted medications, water safety, travel insurance, and vaccination recommendations.
healthcare.costForTourists: Private hospitals in Manila and Cebu provide good care at moderate costs ($50–$150 for consultations). Rural and island healthcare is basic and may require costly medical evacuation for serious conditions.
healthcare.insuranceAdvice: Comprehensive travel insurance with medical evacuation coverage is essential, especially for island-hopping or travel outside major cities where facilities are limited.
healthcare.vaccinationsRecommended: Hepatitis A, typhoid, and routine vaccinations are recommended. Hepatitis B, rabies, and Japanese encephalitis should be considered for longer stays or rural travel. Dengue is a significant risk, especially during rainy season.
healthcare.hospitalNotes: St. Luke's, Makati Medical Center, and other top Manila hospitals provide international-standard care with English-speaking staff. Outside Metro Manila and Cebu, hospital facilities drop off significantly in quality and availability.

commonOTC: motion sickness medication (important for ferry travel)
medications.prescriptionRules: Philippine law requires prescriptions for many medications. Some antibiotics and other drugs that require prescriptions in Western countries are available OTC. For controlled substances, a Philippine prescription is required. Carry your foreign prescription and doctor's letter as backup.

restrictedMeds.name: Diazepam (Valium) and other benzodiazepines
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled substances requiring Philippine prescription. Bring your foreign prescription and doctor's letter. Quantities for personal use are permitted with documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: Codeine-containing medications
restrictedMeds.note: Codeine is controlled. Some codeine preparations may be available OTC in small doses. For larger quantities, a prescription is needed.

restrictedMeds.name: Tramadol
restrictedMeds.note: Controlled opioid. Requires prescription in the Philippines. Bring your documentation.

restrictedMeds.name: ADHD medications (Adderall, Ritalin)
restrictedMeds.note: Strictly controlled. Requires Philippine prescription or special permission from the Philippine Drug Enforcement Agency (PDEA). Contact the embassy before traveling with these medications.

restrictedMeds.name: Medical cannabis
restrictedMeds.note: Cannabis is illegal in the Philippines. Despite some legislative discussions, cannabis remains prohibited. CBD products with no THC are in a legal gray area — avoid bringing them.

medications.bringDocumentation: Carry a doctor's letter in English listing all medications with generic names. Keep medications in original packaging. For any potentially controlled medications, carry the original prescription. Declare all medications at customs.
medications.generalAdvice: The Philippines has strict anti-drug laws with severe penalties including long prison sentences. Common medications are affordable and widely available at pharmacies like Mercury Drug. Carry prescriptions for controlled substances in original packaging with a doctor's letter. Some medications available OTC elsewhere may be restricted — check with the Philippine FDA if unsure about specific drugs.

connectivity.simOptions: Globe or Smart prepaid SIMs at airports and convenience stores. Very cheap — unlimited data promos for PHP 99-299/week. No registration hassle.
connectivity.wifiAvailability: Free WiFi at malls, hotels, and chain restaurants. Speeds can be slow outside Metro Manila. Many islands have limited connectivity.
connectivity.bestOption: Globe prepaid SIM with GoSURF or GOMO data plan. Buy at airport. Coverage good in cities but can be spotty on remote islands.

cultural.tipping: 10% at restaurants if no service charge. Round up for taxis. Tip tour guides and drivers PHP 200-500/day.
cultural.dressCode: Casual and relaxed. Cover up at churches. Swimwear only at beaches/pools. Filipinos dress neatly even casually.
cultural.greetings: Handshake for business. 'Mano po' (touching elder's hand to forehead) shows respect to elders. Smiling is universal. Use 'po' and 'opo' for politeness.
taboos: Raising your voice or showing anger publicly (causes 'loss of face')
Refusing food offered by a host
Pointing with your finger (use lips or eyes to indicate direction)
Arriving exactly on time to social events ('Filipino time' is 15-30 min late)
cultural.haggling: Expected at markets, street vendors, and some small shops. Not at malls or restaurants. Be friendly and respectful.

soloFemaleSafety.note: Solo female travelers are generally treated warmly but should exercise caution with drink safety, avoid isolated areas at night, and be wary of overly friendly strangers in nightlife areas.

lgbtSafety.note: Filipino culture is relatively tolerant of LGBT people and there is a visible LGBT community, but there are no comprehensive anti-discrimination laws and attitudes vary significantly by region.

safety.naturalDisasters: The Philippines is one of the world's most disaster-prone countries, experiencing approximately 20 typhoons annually (peak season June–November), along with earthquakes, volcanic eruptions, and flooding. Travelers should monitor PAGASA weather bulletins and have contingency plans.
safety.pettyCrime: Pickpocketing, bag-snatching, and scams are very common in Manila and other cities, particularly in crowded markets, jeepneys, and tourist areas. Be vigilant with belongings and avoid carrying large amounts of cash.
safety.violentCrime: Armed robbery, kidnapping, and violent crime occur, particularly in Mindanao and the Sulu Archipelago. In Manila and Cebu, express kidnappings and opportunistic armed robberies have been reported, especially targeting those displaying wealth.
safety.notes: Most tourist areas like Boracay, Palawan, and Cebu's resorts are reasonably safe and well-managed. The FCDO and US State Department advise against all travel to western and central Mindanao, the Sulu Archipelago, and the south of the Zamboanga Peninsula due to terrorism and kidnapping risks. Corruption and scams involving police or officials occasionally affect tourists.

practical.visaFreeCountries: US citizens: 30 days visa-free (extendable). UK, EU, Australia also 30 days. Can extend up to 36 months at immigration offices.
practical.bestTimeToVisit: November-May (dry season). December-February best weather. Avoid June-October (typhoon season, especially August-October).

steps: File a police report immediately — get the report number, you will need it
Contact the US Embassy or nearest consulate: Contact the nearest US Embassy
Bring the police report + any ID you have (driver's license, copy of passport)
Apply for an Emergency Passport (usually issued within 1-2 business days)
Notify your travel insurance and airline of the situation
stolenPassport.notes: Keep a digital copy of your passport in cloud storage (Google Photos, iCloud) and email yourself a scan before travel.

steps: Go to the nearest police station (or call 117)
Bring ID or a copy of your passport if available
Request a written report — ask for an English copy or certified translation if needed
Keep the report number safe — required for insurance claims
For theft: list all stolen items with approximate values
policeReport.notes: In many countries, tourist police stations are available in major cities — they have English-speaking staff. Ask your hotel concierge for the nearest tourist police.

steps: If involved in an accident: do not move vehicles if anyone is injured
Call police (117) and ambulance (911) if there are injuries
Exchange contact, license, and insurance details with other parties
Document the scene with photos before moving vehicles
Contact your rental car company's emergency line
Contact your travel insurance's 24h assistance line
roadsideAssistance.notes: Traffic drives on the RIGHT. An International Driving Permit (IDP) is recommended for most foreign licenses. Rental vehicles are available at major airports and cities.

immediate: Monitor PAGASA typhoon warnings — Philippines has the highest typhoon frequency globally
Signal 1: prepare. Signal 2: secure loose items. Signal 3+: evacuate if in flood/storm surge zone
Never ignore Storm Surge warnings — surge can reach 7+ meters and is more deadly than wind
Evacuate to designated evacuation centers when ordered
after: Watch for flooding and landslides in the days after typhoon
Do not cross flooded waterways — leptospirosis risk

immediate: Follow PHIVOLCS alert level system (0-5) for active volcanoes
Alert Level 3+: mandatory evacuation — leave immediately
Wear N95 mask if volcanic ash is falling
Do not enter permanent danger zone (PDZ) around active volcanoes
after: Monitor PHIVOLCS for alert level changes
Do not re-enter evacuated area until PHIVOLCS lowers alert level
